title: Incremental Fact Fluency v2
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Kane presents the second, expanded version of a fact-fluency practice system he built and tested over a year of teaching, covering addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. His central claim is that most fact-fluency failures are failures of practice volume, not of strategy: students who don't practice enough facts don't become fluent, and naive 'just practice more' approaches break down because low-knowledge students answer too few questions per minute while others actively avoid the work. His answer is 'incremental fact fluency' -- breaking each operation into small fact families (like +2s, or the 3s times table), drilling each family in isolation, then interleaving it with everything practiced so far before moving to the next family. He supplements this with 'bridge' worksheets that help students acclimate to a new, harder fact family by explicitly working through and interleaving its neighboring facts, and describes how he sequences instruction, mini-whiteboard checks, and worksheet practice across a class period. Kane is explicit that the materials are 'just pieces of paper' and that they only work if a teacher uses them to make students think hard and build connections between facts, not merely hand them out as busywork. He closes with a pragmatic, non-doctrinaire take on the timed-practice debate, arguing the real lever is smart chunking and connection-building rather than timing itself.
points: The instructional design pattern is 'introduce a fact family, drill it in isolation (blocked practice), then interleave it with everything learned so far' -- repeated incrementally for every fact family in each operation.

Kane's 'Bridge to Multiplication' worksheets specifically address the observed failure mode where students stall and get frustrated at the start of a new, harder fact family, by first having them count up and down through the whole family before mixed practice begins.

The stated goal is not raw memorization for its own sake but freeing working memory: automatic fact recall lets students reason about harder problems without cognitive overload, and connection-building (e.g., deriving 7×4 from 6×4) reduces the amount of rote practice needed.

Kane rejects the binary framing of the timed-practice debate, arguing instructional design -- chunking and connection -- is the variable that determines whether practice produces confidence or avoidance behavior, regardless of whether a timer is used.
quotes: There’s a naive approach that I’ve found helpful but limited: have students practice more. Yes, some students will make progress by just asking them to practice. However, putting fact fluency practice in front of students doesn’t always mean they get enough practice.
I call this approach “incremental fact fluency,” after a research paper that helped to inspire it and the idea that it helps students to learn math facts in manageable, incremental chunks.

The first goal is to familiarize students with the entire fact family. If a student is asked 7 x 4 and can’t retrieve the fact from memory, I want them to know that the answer must be one of the members of the 4 fact family, which narrows the possibilities considerably.

A bedrock principle of learning is that humans learn best when they connect what they are learning to what they already know. Practice is critical to learn one’s math facts, but students need far less practice when the connections between new learning and prior knowledge are emphasized and strengthened.
The pieces of paper will only cause students to learn if the teacher helps students think hard about the problems and make connections.

I don't explicitly time students for two reasons. First, despite the research, I feel cautious about timed practice... Second, I worry that explicit timing reduces the amount of practice for students who answer questions more slowly and most need to improve.
